name: Essential amino acids (EAAs)
lead: Essential amino acids (EAAs) are nine amino acids that humans cannot synthesise fast enough to meet needs and must obtain from food: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine [1]. EAA supplements sell these as a free-form powder, positioned in fitness communities as an alternative to protein powder for muscle building, especially during dieting.

Research shows EAAs stimulate muscle protein synthesis, and a lot of this work centres on leucine content in older adults [2]. Studies on healthy young lifters taking EAA powders versus whole protein for visible physique outcomes are limited in the sources reviewed.

paras: Early 20th-century work showed rats failed on the maize protein zein but recovered with milk casein; William Cumming Rose then identified the essential amino acids, finding ten for rats and eight for adult humans, with histidine later shown essential for adults [1]. Rose used purified amino acid diets in graduate students and measured nitrogen balance [1].

Requirements are expressed per kilogram of body mass per day and have been revised over the past two decades; adult leucine figures are around 39 (WHO) to 42 (US) mg/kg/day [1]. Protein quality depends on essential amino acid balance, and the limiting amino acid determines how well a meal meets needs [1].

Amino acids signal through mTOR [3]. A study in elderly subjects found that a high proportion of leucine was required for optimal stimulation of muscle protein synthesis by essential amino acids [2]. Branched-chain amino acids, the subset of leucine, isoleucine and valine, have been studied for post-exercise soreness and mTOR activation, while an animal literature raises metabolic concerns [4].

The sources reviewed give no human safety data for typical supplement doses. Deficiency of any one essential amino acid inhibits protein synthesis whatever the others supply [1]. BCAA research in mice has raised questions about metabolic and neurological effects that are not established in humans [4].

Registered trials examine EAA-enriched whey with carbohydrate during energy deficit in 17 participants [5], EAAs and protein kinetics during caloric deprivation in 20 [6], and supplementation in sarcopenic obesity in 80 [7]. These populations are people in energy deficit or with muscle loss. No study reviewed tests EAA powders for appearance outcomes.

card.summary: The nine dietary amino acids as a powder; they drive muscle protein synthesis, but aesthetic payoff versus ordinary protein is unstudied.
card.note: No typical-dose human safety data in sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
EAAs are the nine amino acids the body must get from food, sold as a powder.

They stimulate muscle protein synthesis, with leucine central. Evidence compared with ordinary protein for physique is limited.
quick.mechanism: Amino acids, particularly leucine, signal through mTOR to switch on muscle protein synthesis.
quick.risks: Human safety data at typical supplement doses were not found; mouse BCAA work raises open metabolic questions.
